newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Jewish leader drops threat to call Swiss bank boycott.
newsitem.headline: Jewish leader drops threat to call Swiss bank boycott.

text.p: The head of Israel's Jewish Agency on Wednesday dropped his threat to call a boycott of Swiss banks after Switzerland's economics minister apologised for accusing Jewish groups of blackmail.
Avraham Burg told Swiss Television a boycott would not be discussed when Jewish restitution groups meet on February 10.

He said Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz had defused a confrontation between Berne and Jewish groups by apologising for describing Jewish calls for quick compensation of Holocaust victims as "blackmail".
"We said we would consider (a boycott) if Mr Delamuraz did not withdraw his remarks. Now that he has done so, I do not think we will even discuss this," Burg said in an interview.

Bowing to international pressure, Delamuraz wrote to World Jewish Congress head Edgar Bronfman on Tuesday to express his regret for offending Jews with the remark as he finished his one- year term as Swiss president last month.
He said he had been misinformed when he made the accusation last month in a newspaper interview.
Jewish groups have been pressing for compensation in response to charges Swiss banks hoarded wealth deposited by Holocaust victims.
They also want Berne to make amends for Switzerland's anti- Jewish wartime refugee policy that turned back thousands of Jews to near-certain death as the Holocaust raged.

Separately, the head of Switzerland's largest bank said he was confident the bank did not break the law when it shredded old documents despite a ban on destroying records that could help trace Holocaust accounts.
But Union Bank of Switzerland Chairman Robert Studer said he could not rule out entirely the possibility that relevant files had been lost forever.

"Fortunately we can say with nearly 100 percent certainty that what was destroyed was not interesting for the Banking Commission," he told Swiss Television, referring to Switzerland's banking watchdogs.
The government last month forbade banks from destroying any records that could shed light on the funds, but a UBS employee sent some records dating as far back as 1875 to the shredder.
UBS has insisted no client account records were destroyed in the incident, which came to a light when a suspicious security guard passed the documents to Zurich Jewish leaders.
Prosecutors are still investigating the case.
